title: Q1 Attendance Trend: Month-over-Month Change Summary
user_prompt: Using monthly_attendance_summary.csv and ground_truth.json, describe the month-over-month attendance trend for the program across September, October, and November 2025. What was the program-wide attendance rate each month, and how did it change? Identify the direction and approximate magnitude of each monthly change.

gold_facts.claim: Program-wide student attendance rate in September 2025 was 78.71%.
Program-wide student attendance rate in October 2025 was 81.99%.
Program-wide student attendance rate in November 2025 was 82.09%.
The September-to-October attendance change was +3.28 percentage points.
The October-to-November attendance change was +0.10 percentage points, a near-flat month-over-month movement.

gold_insights: Attendance improved meaningfully from September to October (+3.28 pp) but was nearly flat from October to November (+0.10 pp), indicating the trend was not a steady upward progression.
The program ended November below the stated 80% attendance goal threshold in September but above it by October and November.
The non-monotonic, noisy nature of the attendance trend means a simple 'attendance improved each month' narrative overstates the Oct-Nov momentum.
required_limitations: The monthly rates are student-level attendance records aggregated across three schools; school-level variation may differ from the program-wide figure.
Two months of post-baseline data is insufficient to establish a reliable trend; the near-flat Oct-to-Nov change could reflect seasonal factors, schedule changes, or sampling noise.
No causal inference is possible from attendance trend data alone — external factors such as weather, testing weeks, or tutoring schedule changes are not captured in the fixture.
The data covers only one program in one district over three months; results should not be generalized beyond this cohort.
forbidden_claims: Attendance improved steadily each month throughout the quarter.
The attendance trend demonstrates a clean or consistent upward trajectory toward the program goal.
Attendance improvements were caused by any specific programmatic intervention visible in this data.
The October cancellation spike caused the attendance rate to decline in October.
The program achieved its 80% attendance goal in September.

grounding_accuracy.guidance: Verify all three monthly attendance rates and both MoM deltas match ground_truth.json to within tolerance.

insight_quality.guidance: Strong answers note the non-monotonic nature (large Sep-Oct gain, near-flat Oct-Nov) rather than oversimplifying as a consistent upward trend.

evidence_linkage.guidance: Claims should cite ground_truth.json monthly_attendance_rate keys or monthly_attendance_summary.csv rows.

calibration_limitation_handling.guidance: Must acknowledge limited time window, school-level heterogeneity, and absence of causal explanation.

title: October Satisfaction Dip: Executive Snapshot with Caveats
user_prompt: Using monthly_satisfaction_summary.csv and ground_truth.json, prepare an executive-level snapshot of the student satisfaction trend across the Q1 reporting period (September–November 2025). Focus on the parent feedback and student satisfaction survey types. Include the average scores by month, characterize the October dip, and note any recovery in November. What limitations should be communicated to leadership alongside these figures?

gold_facts.claim: Parent feedback average score in September 2025 was 3.88 (on a 5-point scale).
Parent feedback average score dropped to 3.45 in October 2025, a decline of approximately 0.43 points.
Parent feedback average score recovered to 3.87 in November 2025.
Student satisfaction average score in October 2025 was 3.38, down from 3.88 in September.
Student satisfaction recovered to 3.87 in November 2025.

gold_insights: All three survey types (parent feedback, student satisfaction, tutor self-evaluation) showed a concurrent dip in October and partial-to-full recovery in November, suggesting the dip was program-wide rather than limited to a single respondent group.
November scores rebounded strongly but remained below the program's stated 4.0 satisfaction goal for student satisfaction, meaning the goal was not met at quarter close.
The pattern of dip-then-recovery is consistent with a transient disruption in October rather than a sustained decline.
required_limitations: Survey response rates vary by month and survey type; the parent feedback response rate was below 50% in some months, which may bias averages.

The co-occurrence of the October satisfaction dip and the October session cancellation spike does not establish that cancellations caused the satisfaction drop — other unmeasured factors may have contributed.
Tutor self-evaluation has only 6 respondents per month, too small a sample to draw statistically reliable conclusions.
Parent surveys were noted in program_context.json as having delayed administration due to translation needs; early-quarter satisfaction may be underrepresented.
No benchmark or comparison program satisfaction data is available in this pack to contextualize whether these scores are high, low, or typical.
forbidden_claims: The October session cancellations caused the satisfaction dip.
Satisfaction declined because of tutor performance issues.
The program achieved its 4.0 student satisfaction goal by the end of the quarter.
The recovery in November means the October disruption had no lasting effect on families or students.
Parent satisfaction scores are representative of all enrolled families.

grounding_accuracy.guidance: All five monthly satisfaction averages must match monthly_satisfaction_summary.csv / ground_truth.json within tolerance.

insight_quality.guidance: Strong answers note the cross-survey-type concurrence of the dip, the partial recovery pattern, and the unmet 4.0 goal.

evidence_linkage.guidance: Each monthly figure should be traceable to a specific row in monthly_satisfaction_summary.csv.

calibration_limitation_handling.guidance: Must explicitly refuse causal attribution between cancellations and satisfaction dip; must note response rate limitations.

title: October Cancellation Spike: What the Data Shows and Does Not Show
user_prompt: Using monthly_attendance_summary.csv and ground_truth.json, analyze the October 2025 session cancellation pattern. What was the cancellation rate in October compared to September and November? What can and cannot be concluded from the data about why the spike occurred or what effect it had on student outcomes?

gold_facts.claim: The program-wide session cancellation rate in October 2025 was 27.89%.
The September 2025 cancellation rate was 10.64%.
The November 2025 cancellation rate was 9.52%.
October had 53 cancelled sessions out of 190 scheduled across all three schools.

gold_insights: The October cancellation rate of 27.89% was more than 2.5 times the September rate and nearly 3 times the November rate, making it a clear statistical outlier within the quarter.
The cancellation spike was concentrated in one month and did not persist into November, suggesting it reflected a transient disruption rather than a structural scheduling problem.
Program context notes mention schedule conflicts as a possible contributor to elevated October cancellations, but this is contextual commentary, not causal evidence from the data files.
required_limitations: The fixture data records that cancellations occurred in October but does not record the reason for individual cancellations; causal attribution to any specific factor is speculative.

The program_context.json mentions schedule conflicts as an implementation challenge, but this is narrative context provided by the program — it is not independently verified in the session or attendance data.
Without student-level outcome data (test scores, learning progression), the effect of missed sessions on learning cannot be determined from attendance data alone.
Three months of data does not allow distinguishing a true seasonal pattern from a one-time event.
forbidden_claims: The elevated October cancellations caused the student satisfaction dip in October.
Schedule conflicts have been confirmed as the cause of the October cancellation spike.
The cancellation spike harmed student learning outcomes.
The lower cancellation rate in November means the program fully recovered from the October disruption.
Cancellations in one school were more responsible than others for the spike.

grounding_accuracy.guidance: Cancellation rates for all three months and total October cancelled sessions must match ground_truth.json / monthly_attendance_summary.csv.

insight_quality.guidance: Strong answers quantify the spike as a ratio/multiple of other months and note its transience.

evidence_linkage.guidance: October cancelled session counts should cite specific rows (MAS-0004, MAS-0005, MAS-0006) from monthly_attendance_summary.csv.

calibration_limitation_handling.guidance: Must explicitly disclaim causal attribution between cancellations and satisfaction, and between cancellations and learning outcomes.

title: Program-Wide Q1 Attendance Snapshot Against Stated Goals
user_prompt: Using ground_truth.json and monthly_attendance_summary.csv, write a brief program snapshot addressing whether the tutoring program met its stated attendance goal of ≥80% for Q1 (September–November 2025). Report the program-wide quarterly attendance rate and each monthly rate. Describe what the data shows about goal attainment and flag any caveats for a program director audience.

gold_facts.claim: The program-wide attendance rate across Q1 was 80.92%.
September 2025 attendance rate was 78.71%, below the ≥80% goal.
October 2025 attendance rate was 81.99%, above the ≥80% goal.
November 2025 attendance rate was 82.09%, above the ≥80% goal.

gold_insights: The quarterly aggregate (80.92%) narrowly clears the 80% attendance goal, but this masks the below-goal September baseline — the program was not above target for the full quarter.
Month-level attendance was below goal only in September; both October and November exceeded 80%, suggesting a meaningful improvement from program launch.
A quarterly average that barely clears the goal threshold should be communicated cautiously; small changes in the September baseline would have placed the program below its annual target.
required_limitations: The 80.92% quarterly rate is an average across three schools with different enrollment sizes; school-level rates vary and some schools may remain below goal even when the aggregate is above it.
The attendance goal of ≥80% is stated in program_context.json as a program target; whether the 80% threshold was defined at the monthly or quarterly level is not specified in the data.
Student-level attendance rates (ground_truth.json) differ from session-completion rates (monthly_attendance_summary.csv); the two measures can diverge due to group session structure.
Data covers only Q1; three months is insufficient to establish whether the attendance trend will be sustained.
forbidden_claims: The program fully met its attendance goal across all months.
The program will sustain above-80% attendance in future quarters based on this trend.
September attendance was below goal because the program was just launching and students were not yet engaged.
The school-level variation in attendance rates is trivial or negligible.
The attendance goal has been definitively achieved for the year.

grounding_accuracy.guidance: All four numeric facts (three monthly rates and the quarterly aggregate) must match ground_truth.json within tolerance.

insight_quality.guidance: Strong answers note the below-goal September and the narrow aggregate margin, not just the headline 80.92% figure.

evidence_linkage.guidance: The quarterly rate claim should cite ground_truth.json program_wide_attendance_rate; monthly rates should cite monthly_attendance_rate keys.

calibration_limitation_handling.guidance: Must note that aggregate goal attainment masks a below-goal month, and should flag measurement ambiguity between student-level and session-level rates.

title: Multi-Signal October Snapshot: Correlating Cancellations, Attendance, and Satisfaction
user_prompt: Using monthly_attendance_summary.csv, monthly_satisfaction_summary.csv, and ground_truth.json, produce an integrated snapshot of October 2025 across three signals: session cancellation rate, student attendance rate, and student satisfaction score. For each signal, state the October value, compare it to September, and note whether the direction of change was consistent across signals. What interpretive cautions should accompany this multi-signal view?

gold_facts.claim: October 2025 session cancellation rate was 27.89%, up from 10.64% in September (+17.25 pp).
October 2025 student attendance rate was 81.99%, up from 78.71% in September (+3.28 pp).
October 2025 student satisfaction (student survey) average score was 3.38, down from 3.88 in September (-0.50 points).
October 2025 parent feedback average score was 3.45, down from 3.88 in September (-0.43 points).

gold_insights: In October 2025, cancellations and satisfaction moved in the same direction (cancellations up, satisfaction down) while student attendance moved in the opposite direction (attendance up) — the three signals did not tell a uniform story.

The co-occurrence of elevated cancellations and lower satisfaction in October is an observable correlation in the data, but the fixture data does not contain the information needed to determine whether cancellations influenced satisfaction or whether a common third factor affected both.

An integrated multi-signal snapshot must acknowledge that student attendance and session cancellation rate measure different constructs: attendance reflects individual student presence at scheduled sessions, while cancellation rate reflects sessions removed before they occurred.
required_limitations: Correlation between elevated October cancellations and lower October satisfaction does not establish causation; the data does not record why satisfaction declined.
The attendance and cancellation metrics are derived from different base denominators (student-session records vs. scheduled sessions), which limits direct comparison.
Satisfaction survey response rates fluctuated across months and remain below 65% for all survey types; non-response bias may affect the averages.
All signals are aggregated at the program level; school-level or subgroup-level variation is masked in these monthly summaries.
Three months of data provides a very limited baseline for interpreting whether any October signal value was anomalous relative to a longer historical pattern.
forbidden_claims: The October cancellation spike caused student satisfaction to decline.
Higher attendance in October despite cancellations means students were unaffected by the session disruptions.
The negative correlation between cancellations and satisfaction proves a causal relationship.
October was universally a worse month than September across all program signals.
The simultaneous dip in satisfaction and rise in cancellations can be attributed to a single root cause.

grounding_accuracy.guidance: All four October numeric values (cancellation rate, attendance rate, student satisfaction, parent feedback) must match ground_truth.json within tolerance.

insight_quality.guidance: Strong answers explicitly note the directional inconsistency (attendance up, satisfaction down) and resist oversimplifying October as uniformly worse.

evidence_linkage.guidance: Each signal value should be traced to the appropriate source file and field (e.g., ground_truth.json monthly_cancellation_rate vs monthly_attendance_rate).

calibration_limitation_handling.guidance: Must explicitly reject causal attribution between cancellations and satisfaction; must note that the two metrics measure different constructs.
